title: Aggregation
summary: Master weak 'has-a' aggregation where parts belong to a whole but survive independently if the whole is destroyed.
learningObjectives: Define Aggregation as a specialized whole-part relationship with independent lifecycles
Identify real-world aggregation examples (Department & Teachers, Playlist & Songs)
Implement aggregation in Java using constructor injection of externally created objects
Contrast aggregation with composition regarding garbage collection and lifecycle management
expectedOutcomes: You can model whole-part systems where the child objects outlive the parent container
You can choose aggregation when parts need to be shared across multiple containers

activities.title: Practical Context: Loose Whole-Part Containment

realWorldMetaphor.scenario: Consider the Computer Science Department at a university and Professor Turing who teaches there. The Department HAS professors. However, if budget cuts shut down the Department, Professor Turing does not vanish from existence! She simply transfers to the Mathematics Department or writes research papers independently.
realWorldMetaphor.mapping: In OOP, `Department` aggregates `Teacher` objects. The `Department` holds references to teachers created elsewhere. If the `Department` object is deleted or garbage-collected, the `Teacher` objects continue living in memory because they were created externally.
realWorldMetaphor.takeaway: In aggregation, the whole HAS parts, but the parts have an independent existence and lifecycle.

activities.content:
Many systems represent collections where a container groups external components, but the components exist independently outside of that container.

For example, a University Department contains Professors:
- If the Department closes down, the Professors do not cease to exist—they can transfer to another department.

Aggregation models this weak ownership relationship where the whole contains parts without controlling their lifecycles.

activities.title: Aggregation in Java: Definition, Syntax, and The Weak Has-A Relationship
Music Playlist Aggregating Independent Songs
activities.explanation: Song instances exist independently of Playlist. Multiple playlists can aggregate the exact same Song instance simultaneously.

stepByStepWalkthrough.description: `roadTrip` also aggregates `s1`, proving shared existence across containers.
Destroying one playlist leaves the songs intact for other playlists.

activities.title: Sports League and Players Aggregation
activities.explanation: Athletes are created prior to Team construction and passed into Team. Athletes can change teams or play for national teams.

stepByStepWalkthrough.description: `Athlete` objects are created independently on the heap.
`Team` constructor receives the external list of athletes.
`Team` shallow-copies the collection into its internal roster.
The athletes outlive any single season or team disbandment.

questions.question: What happens to the aggregated 'parts' when the 'whole' is garbage collected?
options: They are automatically deleted as well
They continue to exist if references to them are held elsewhere
The JVM throws a BrokenAggregationException
They are moved into Metaspace
questions.explanation: In aggregation, parts have independent lifecycles. They are not destroyed when the containing whole is destroyed.

questions.question: How is aggregation depicted in UML class diagrams?
options: A solid black filled diamond on the whole
A hollow (clear) diamond on the whole
A dotted arrow
A double-headed green arrow
questions.explanation: Aggregation is represented by a hollow (unfilled) diamond at the container class end.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most classic textbook example of Aggregation?
options: Human and Heart
Building and Rooms
Department and Teachers
Car and Engine block casting
questions.explanation: A Teacher can exist without a Department (and can move between departments), making it aggregation.

questions.question: How are aggregated objects typically supplied to the container in Java?
options: Instantiated directly using 'new' inside the private fields
Passed into the container via constructor or setter (Dependency Injection)
Cloned via native bytecode
Defined as static final constants
questions.explanation: In aggregation, components are created externally and injected into the container via constructors or setter methods.

questions.question: Can an aggregated object belong to more than one container at the same time?
options: Yes, because it is an independent object referenced by multiple containers
No, Java memory model restricts an object to one container
Only if it is a primitive type
Only if both containers are in the same package
questions.explanation: Multiple containers can hold reference pointers to the same aggregated instance simultaneously (e.g. Song in multiple Playlists).

questions.question: Why is aggregation called 'Weak Has-A'?
options: Because it runs slower than inheritance
Because there is no strong ownership of the part's lifecycle by the whole
Because it uses weak references (java.lang.ref.WeakReference)
Because the code is prone to syntax errors
questions.explanation: It is 'weak' because the whole does not own or terminate the lifecycle of the part.

questions.question: If a Library closes down, what happens to the Books in an aggregation model?
options: The books can be donated, moved to another library, or read individually
The books must be destroyed
The books turn into null
The JVM crashes
questions.explanation: Because Books are aggregated, they exist independently of whether the Library entity is active or destroyed.

questions.question: Which access pattern preserves the integrity of an aggregated list inside a container?
options: Return the raw mutable List directly from getter
Return Collections.unmodifiableList(...) from getter
Make the List public
Delete the List after viewing
questions.explanation: Returning Collections.unmodifiableList(...) prevents external callers from modifying the container's internal list.

questions.question: What distinguishes Aggregation from simple Association?
options: Aggregation implies a whole-part relationship, whereas simple association is a generic peer relationship
Aggregation uses extends, association does not
Association uses interfaces only
They are identical in every way
questions.explanation: Aggregation specifically implies a container-containee (whole-part) concept, while association can be any generic relationship.

questions.question: In Java code, what is the key syntactic difference between Aggregation and Composition?
options: Aggregation uses 'new Component()' inside the container; Composition takes Component as parameter
Aggregation receives Component from outside; Composition creates Component internally using 'new'
Aggregation requires the final keyword
Composition requires the static keyword
questions.explanation: Aggregation accepts externally instantiated components; Composition instantiates its components internally to bind their lifecycles.

questions.question: How do you distinguish Aggregation from Composition in a system design interview?
questions.answer: Ask: 'If the container object is deleted, should the child objects still exist?' If yes, it is Aggregation (e.g. a Company and its Employees—if the company goes bankrupt, employees still exist). If no, it is Composition (e.g. an Order and its OrderItems—deleting an order destroys its line items).
questions.expectedAnswer: Ask: 'If the container object is deleted, should the child objects still exist?' If yes, it is Aggregation (e.g. a Company and its Employees—if the company goes bankrupt, employees still exist). If no, it is Composition (e.g. an Order and its OrderItems—deleting an order destroys its line items).
questions.keyTakeaway: Test of lifecycle dependency: survival of parts = Aggregation; destruction of parts = Composition.
keyPoints: Test of lifecycle dependency: survival of parts = Aggregation; destruction of parts = Composition.

questions.question: How does Aggregation facilitate testing and mocking?
questions.answer: Because aggregated dependencies are injected from outside (via constructor or setter), unit tests can easily inject mock implementations (e.g. Mockito mocks) instead of real production objects, enabling fast, isolated tests.
questions.expectedAnswer: Because aggregated dependencies are injected from outside (via constructor or setter), unit tests can easily inject mock implementations (e.g. Mockito mocks) instead of real production objects, enabling fast, isolated tests.
questions.keyTakeaway: Aggregation directly aligns with Dependency Injection, making classes inherently testable.
keyPoints: Aggregation directly aligns with Dependency Injection, making classes inherently testable.

questions.question: Can an object participate in both Aggregation and Composition at the same time in different contexts?
questions.answer: Yes! An `Engine` is aggregated by a `MechanicWorkshop` (which services many engines that come and go), but composed by a `Car` (which owns and manages that specific engine's lifecycle). Context determines the relationship.
questions.expectedAnswer: Yes! An `Engine` is aggregated by a `MechanicWorkshop` (which services many engines that come and go), but composed by a `Car` (which owns and manages that specific engine's lifecycle). Context determines the relationship.
questions.keyTakeaway: Relationships are defined by context and domain architecture, not fixed to a class in isolation.
keyPoints: Relationships are defined by context and domain architecture, not fixed to a class in isolation.

questions.question: What is the UML distinction between Aggregation and Composition?
questions.answer: Aggregation is drawn with a hollow white diamond on the container class. Composition is drawn with a solid black filled diamond on the container class.
questions.expectedAnswer: Aggregation is drawn with a hollow white diamond on the container class. Composition is drawn with a solid black filled diamond on the container class.
questions.keyTakeaway: Hollow diamond = Aggregation (weak). Filled diamond = Composition (strong).
keyPoints: Hollow diamond = Aggregation (weak). Filled diamond = Composition (strong).

questions.question: Why should you return an unmodifiable view when exposing aggregated collections?
questions.answer: If you return `this.teachers` directly, external callers can call `.clear()` or add invalid elements, violating encapsulation. Returning `Collections.unmodifiableList(teachers)` protects the container's internal integrity while allowing read access.
questions.expectedAnswer: If you return `this.teachers` directly, external callers can call `.clear()` or add invalid elements, violating encapsulation. Returning `Collections.unmodifiableList(teachers)` protects the container's internal integrity while allowing read access.
questions.keyTakeaway: Always return unmodifiable views or defensive copies of internal collections.
keyPoints: Always return unmodifiable views or defensive copies of internal collections.

questions.question: How does garbage collection behave when an aggregated container is dereferenced?
questions.answer: When the container is dereferenced, its internal reference pointer to the parts is cleared. If external references to the parts still exist (like in a caller or another container), the parts remain safely in the JVM heap.
questions.expectedAnswer: When the container is dereferenced, its internal reference pointer to the parts is cleared. If external references to the parts still exist (like in a caller or another container), the parts remain safely in the JVM heap.
questions.keyTakeaway: JVM garbage collection preserves any object reachable from living root references.
keyPoints: JVM garbage collection preserves any object reachable from living root references.

practiceProblems.title: Department and Professor Aggregation
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Complete the `Department` class to aggregate `Professor` objects. The professors are created externally and passed into the department. Complete `Department.addProfessor` and `Department.printDirectory` to output each professor's name and specialty.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Faculty Directory: Computer Science
 * Dr. Alan Turing [Computation]
 * Dr. Ada Lovelace [Algorithms]

practiceProblems.title: Music Playlist Multi-Container Sharing
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Demonstrate that aggregated objects can belong to multiple containers simultaneously from scratch:
1. Class `Track`: holds `private String isrc` and `private String title`. Constructor initializes both. Method `public String getDisplay()` returns title + ' (' + isrc + ')'.
2. Class `MusicPlaylist`: holds `private String name` and `private java.util.List<Track> tracks = new java.util.ArrayList<>()`.
   - Constructor initializes name.
   - Method `public void addTrack(Track t)` adds track.
   - Method `public void showTracklist()` prints `'=== Playlist: ' + name + ' ==='` then each track as `' - ' + t.getDisplay()`.
3. In `Main`, create Track t1 ('US-100', 'Midnight City') and Track t2 ('US-200', 'Starlight').
4. Create Playlist 'Favorites' with t1 and t2. Create Playlist 'Night Drive' with t1 only.
5. Call `showTracklist()` on both playlists.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
=== Playlist: Favorites ===
 - Midnight City (US-100)
 - Starlight (US-200)
=== Playlist: Night Drive ===
 - Midnight City (US-100)
hints: Notice t1 is added to both favs and night.

practiceProblems.title: Software Project Team Aggregating Engineers
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Build a software project aggregation model from scratch:
1. Class `SoftwareEngineer`: holds `private String name` and `private String role`. Constructor initializes both. Method `public String getBadge()` returns name + ' [' + role + ']'.
2. Class `EngineeringTeam`: holds `private String projectCodename` and `private java.util.List<SoftwareEngineer> members = new java.util.ArrayList<>()`.
   - Constructor initializes projectCodename.
   - Method `public void recruit(SoftwareEngineer eng)` adds to members.
   - Method `public void disbandTeam()`: prints `'Disbanding team for project: ' + projectCodename`. Clears `members`. Prints `'Team cleared. Engineers remain active in company pool.'`.
   - Method `public int getMemberCount()` returns members.size().
3. In `Main`, create Engineer 'Linus' ('Architect') and Engineer 'Ken' ('Systems'). Create team 'Project Apollo'. Recruit both. Print member count (2). Call `disbandTeam()`. Print Linus's badge to confirm he still exists.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Active members: 2
Disbanding team for project: Project Apollo
Team cleared. Engineers remain active in company pool.
Survivor: Linus [Architect]
hints: Even after team.disbandTeam() clears the list, e1 remains intact in main.
This demonstrates weak aggregation lifecycle independence.

practiceProblems.title: Bug Hunt: Leaking Mutable Aggregated List
practiceProblems.problemStatement: The following `ArtGallery` class accidentally returns its internal mutable list of `Painting`s. An external rogue function clears the list from the outside, destroying the gallery's internal records! Fix `ArtGallery.getPaintings()` to return an unmodifiable view using `java.util.Collections.unmodifiableList(paintings)` so the gallery cannot be tampered with from outside.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Gallery protected: Modification rejected!
Exhibits count: 1
hints: This throws UnsupportedOperationException when add is attempted.

practiceProblems.title: Air Traffic Control Fleet Airspace Aggregation
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Build an Air Traffic Control (ATC) radar sector aggregating aircraft from scratch:
1. Class `CommercialAircraft`: holds `private String callsign`, `private int altitudeFt`, and `private int speedKnots`. Constructor initializes all three. Method `public String getRadarBlip()` returns `'[' + callsign + '] Alt: ' + altitudeFt + 'ft, Spd: ' + speedKnots + 'kts'`.
2. Class `RadarSector`: holds `private String sectorId` and `private java.util.List<CommercialAircraft> trackedAircraft = new java.util.ArrayList<>()`.
   - Constructor initializes sectorId.
   - Method `public void handoffIn(CommercialAircraft ac)` adds aircraft.
   - Method `public void handoffOut(CommercialAircraft ac)` removes aircraft.
   - Method `public void scanSector()` prints `'=== Radar Sweep Sector: ' + sectorId + ' ==='`. If empty, prints `'Sector Clear'`. Otherwise prints each blip indented with `' > ' + blip`.
3. In `Main`, create aircraft UA101 (32000ft, 450kts) and DL404 (28000ft, 420kts). Create Sector 'SECTOR-ZNY'. Handoff both in. Run `scanSector()`. Handoff UA101 out. Run `scanSector()` again to observe DL404 remaining.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
=== Radar Sweep Sector: SECTOR-ZNY ===
 > [UA101] Alt: 32000ft, Spd: 450kts
 > [DL404] Alt: 28000ft, Spd: 420kts
=== Radar Sweep Sector: SECTOR-ZNY ===
 > [DL404] Alt: 28000ft, Spd: 420kts
hints: Aircraft are created in main and enter/exit sectors seamlessly.
Removing UA101 from trackedAircraft leaves DL404 intact.
